title: Suspected Meningitis and Encephalitis: ED Investigation and Treatment Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with suspected bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis in the emergency department (ED): early antibiotics, dexamethasone, blood tests, computed tomography (CT) before lumbar puncture criteria, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests, aciclovir for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis and duration by organism.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG240 gives no numeric doses and defers to the British National Formulary; adult doses come from two Scottish health board guidelines (NHS Grampian and NHS Tayside) and have not been compared with the British National Formulary or a Saudi protocol.
No Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) meningitis guideline was opened; local microbiology and infection specialist advice apply.
CSF numeric thresholds (cell count, protein, glucose ratio) were not given in the sources opened; use the laboratory's age-specific ranges.

Vancomycin and rifampicin are mentioned by NHS Tayside for travel-related resistance with no dose in the opened extract other than a trough target of 15–20 mg/L; they are listed as specialist-advice only.
Renal and hepatic adjustments for ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, dexamethasone, co-trimoxazole, chloramphenicol and meropenem are not given in the sources opened.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Bacterial infection of the meninges causes inflammation; empirical antibiotics are chosen to cover the likely organisms and Listeria in at-risk adults. Inflammation can raise intracranial pressure; the NICE guideline lists new focal neurological features, abnormal pupils and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 9 or less as signs that call for imaging first. Meningococcal disease can cause septic shock with a non-blanching rash; lumbar puncture is not done with extensive or rapidly spreading purpura. Herpes simplex virus is the strongest viral encephalitis suspicion and is treated with intravenous aciclovir. Antibiotic therapy given before lumbar puncture can reduce the reliability of CSF culture, so blood cultures and whole-blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are taken first.

physicalSigns: New focal neurological signs or abnormal pupillary reactions.
Signs of sepsis such as tachycardia and hypotension.
redFlags: GCS score of 9 or less, or a progressive, sustained or rapid fall in consciousness.
New focal neurological features including seizures or posturing, or abnormal pupillary reactions.
Shock, unprotected airway, respiratory compromise or uncontrolled seizures.
precipitants: Age 60 years or over, pregnancy or immunocompromise (including alcohol dependency, diabetes or malignancy): Listeria risk per NHS Grampian.
Recent travel to areas of high antibiotic resistance within 6 months (NHS Tayside).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Non-blanching rash with shock; give ceftriaxone and do not delay for lumbar puncture.
Milder illness; CSF PCR positive; antibiotics stopped when bacterial infection is excluded.
Altered behaviour, seizures; CSF herpes simplex virus PCR; aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours.
Focal signs, raised pressure signs; CT before lumbar puncture.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and stabilise
actions: Treat suspected bacterial meningitis as an emergency; stabilise an unprotected airway, respiratory compromise, shock, uncontrolled seizures or bleeding risk before lumbar puncture.
Take blood culture, white cell count, CRP or procalcitonin, glucose, lactate and whole-blood PCR.

clinicalManagement.title: Give antibiotics and dexamethasone
actions: Give ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 12 hours; add amoxicillin 2 g intravenously every 4 hours if Listeria risk.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg intravenously every 6 hours for 4 days with or just before the first antibiotic dose to adults with suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis; stop if the organism is not pneumococcus or Haemophilus influenzae type b.
Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging; immediate antimicrobial therapy should be given before lumbar puncture if there is any delay.

clinicalManagement.title: Decide on imaging and lumbar puncture
actions: Do CT first only when the NICE imaging criteria are met; do not do lumbar puncture if contraindicated.
If antibiotics have started, perform lumbar puncture as soon as it is safe.

clinicalManagement.title: Cover for encephalitis
actions: Add aciclovir 10 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours only if herpes simplex encephalitis is strongly suspected; NICE does not routinely recommend it for meningitis.
Continue for 14 days (21 days if immunocompromised) then repeat lumbar puncture.

clinicalManagement.title: Narrow by organism and set duration
actions: Pneumococcus: ceftriaxone for 10 days. Meningococcus: 5 days. Haemophilus influenzae type b: 7 days. Group B streptococcus: 14 days. Enterobacterales: 21 days. Listeria: 21 days of amoxicillin.
Culture-negative with CSF suggesting bacterial meningitis: 10 days.
Agree total duration with the infection specialist.

clinicalManagement.title: Support and escalate
actions: Do not restrict fluids below maintenance; do not use glycerol; do not routinely use mannitol or hypertonic saline.
Seek urgent critical care advice for suspected raised pressure; do not routinely use invasive intracranial pressure monitoring.
Notify public health; contact prophylaxis follows national public health advice.

regimens.indication: Empirical treatment of suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis
regimens.duration: Organism dependent: 5 days meningococcus, 10 days pneumococcus, 7 days Haemophilus influenzae type b, 14 days group B streptococcus, 21 days Enterobacterales; 10 days if culture-negative
adjustments: No renal or hepatic adjustment is given in the sources opened; check product information.
NICE: use cefotaxime if ceftriaxone is contraindicated.
monitoring: Clinical review for response; agree total duration with the infection specialist.
contraindications: Severe allergy to ceftriaxone: use chloramphenicol-based regimen per specialist advice.
Non-severe penicillin allergy: ceftriaxone can still be used (NICE).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: New focal neurological features, abnormal pupillary reactions, GCS 9 or less or rapid fall, or a risk of an evolving space-occupying lesion.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Do not do lumbar puncture (NICE NG240)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Extensive or rapidly spreading purpura, infection at the puncture site, space-occupying lesion risk, or raised intracranial pressure signs until resolved.
Intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of hospital arrival, after blood samples and lumbar puncture where lumbar puncture is safe and not delaying.

guidelineComparison.title: Adult empirical bacterial meningitis regimens in the two Scottish guidelines

values: Chloramphenicol 25 mg/kg IV four times daily.
10 mg IV every 6 hours; duration with infection specialist.

guidelineComparison.note: The two sources agree; NICE NG240 gives no numeric doses.

teaching.scope: Adult with suspected bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis in the emergency department (ED): early antibiotics, dexamethasone, blood tests, computed tomography (CT) before lumbar puncture criteria, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests, aciclovir for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis and duration by organism.
learningObjectives: Give antibiotics within 1 hour; do not delay for imaging or puncture.
Apply the NICE criteria for CT before lumbar puncture.
Dose and duration antibiotics by organism.
pitfalls: Omitting Listeria cover in at-risk adults.
Forgetting aciclovir when encephalitis is suspected.
keyPoints: Antibiotics before lumbar puncture if any delay.
A normal CRP does not exclude bacterial meningitis.
Dexamethasone stops if organism is not pneumococcus or Haemophilus influenzae type b.
